title: Given an image as a grid of pixel colors, a starting pixel, and a new color, repaint the starting pixel and all connected pixels of the same original color with the new color, where connectivity is orthogonal. Return the modified image.
shortTitle: Flood Fill — BFS/DFS from starting cell
topicTitle: Given an image as a grid of pixel colors

s1_definition.profdef: Flood Fill performs a traversal from the starting cell, recoloring every orthogonally connected cell that shares the starting cell's original color. It stops at cells of a different color or at the grid boundary, and guards against reprocessing by checking the new color or using a visited set, especially when the new color equals the original.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of recoloring a contiguous region on a dashboard heat map. You click a tile and want every connected tile of the same current status to switch to a new status. You spread outward from the clicked tile, flipping each same-status neighbor, and stop where the status differs, being careful not to loop when the new status matches the old.
s1_definition.oneliner: From the start cell, DFS or BFS recoloring all connected cells of the original color, stopping at different colors and guarding against the no-op case where new equals old.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Flood Fill performs a traversal from the starting cell, recoloring every orthogonally connected cell that shares the starting cell's original color. It stops at cells of a different color or at the grid boundary, and guards against reprocessing by checking the new color or using a visited set, especially when the new color equals the original.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of recoloring a contiguous region on a dashboard heat map. You click a tile and want every connected tile of the same current status to switch to a new status. You spread outward from the clicked tile, flipping each same-status neighbor, and stop where the status differs, being careful not to loop when the new status matches the old.

**One line to remember:** From the start cell, DFS or BFS recoloring all connected cells of the original color, stopping at different colors and guarding against the no-op case where new equals old.

sections.s2_technical:
Record the starting cell's original color. If the new color equals the original, return immediately, because repainting would be a no-op and a naive search could loop forever. For example: `if (image[sr][sc] == newColor) return image;`.

Otherwise run a traversal from the start, and for each cell whose color equals the original, set it to the new color and recurse or enqueue its four neighbors. For example: `image[r][c] = newColor; fill(up); fill(down); fill(left); fill(right);`. Cells of a different color and out-of-bounds positions stop the spread.

Because a repainted cell no longer matches the original color, it will not be processed again, so the new color itself acts as the visited marker, which is why the equal-color guard at the start is essential. For example: `if (image[r][c] != original) return;`.

The time is linear in the number of cells in the connected region, and the space is bounded by that region for the stack or queue. A senior nuance is the guard against new equaling original to avoid infinite recursion, and the choice of BFS for very large regions to avoid deep recursion, mirroring the island problem but with an arbitrary start cell rather than a full grid sweep.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a risk heat map lets an analyst reclassify a contiguous region of same-status cells by clicking one cell. The system must repaint the whole connected same-status region. This is exactly how Flood Fill works — spread from the start cell over the matching color.

Problem 2 — Reclassifying to the same status must be a safe no-op, not an infinite loop. This is exactly why the equal-color guard is used.

The mini-project builds a `HeatMapFiller` using DFS flood fill, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo over a status grid.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is a three-by-three status grid, a start at the center cell one-one with original status one, and a new status two.

Step 1: The original status at the center is one, and the new status two differs, so the fill proceeds past the guard.

Step 2: The center cell is repainted to two, then its four neighbors are explored.

Step 3: The up, left, and right neighbors all have status one, so they are repainted to two and their neighbors explored in turn.

Step 4: The spread reaches the entire connected block of status-one cells in the top rows and left column, repainting each to two.

Step 5: Cells with status zero, such as one-two and two-one, stop the spread because they differ from the original.

Step 6: The disconnected status-one cell at two-two, cut off by zeros, is never reached and keeps its value. The connected region is now all two.

```text
2026-10-26T22:20:00Z [INFO] National Bank of India — Risk Heat Map Reclassify
2026-10-26T22:20:00Z [INFO] Filled region; result=[[2, 2, 2], [2, 2, 0], [2, 0, 1]]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  start (1,1)=1, newStatus=2, original=1

    1 1 1          2 2 2
    1 1 0    ──►   2 2 0
    1 0 1          2 0 1   (bottom-right 1 is cut off by 0s → unchanged)

  spread over connected '1's only; '0' cells stop the fill;
  guard: if newStatus==original → return (no infinite loop)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Flood Fill asks me to recolor a connected region of a grid starting from a clicked cell, repainting every orthogonally connected cell that shares the start cell's original color. My solution records the original color, then runs a depth-first or breadth-first search from the start that repaints each matching cell and spreads to its four neighbors, stopping at cells of a different color and at the grid boundary.

The single most important detail is the guard at the top: if the new color already equals the original color, I return immediately. Without this guard, a naive search would repaint cells to a color that still matches the original condition and could loop forever. With distinct colors, a repainted cell no longer matches the original, so the new color itself serves as the visited marker and no cell is processed twice.

This is linear in the size of the connected region, with stack or queue space bounded by that region. For very large regions I prefer BFS to avoid deep recursion. The problem is essentially the island traversal but seeded from one arbitrary cell instead of sweeping the whole grid, which is a connection I point out to show I see the shared pattern.

In my project at National Bank of India, a risk heat map let an analyst reclassify a contiguous block of same-status cells by clicking one cell. Flood fill spread the new status across the connected region and stopped at cells of a different status, while the equal-status guard made reclassifying to the same value a safe no-op rather than an infinite loop, so the tool behaved predictably on every click.
